title: Networking
description: Wide area networks, wireless, IP addressing, converged protocols, network authentication, network attacks, virtualization and common network commands.

nodes.title: WAN
nodes.description:
Networks spread over a large geographical area, such as an entire country, a continent or the world.
Several protocols have been created over the years to enable them. Know these.
Full name: Wide Area Networks.

children.title: X.25
children.description:
One of the first protocol suites for packet-switched networks across a WAN.
First published in 1976, before IPv4 and the OSI model.

children.title: Frame Relay
children.description:
A packet-switched WAN protocol that mostly replaced X.25.
Customers share the carrier's network through virtual circuits, and pay for a committed information rate (CIR).

children.title: ATM
children.description:
A WAN protocol that sends data in small, fixed-size cells.
Mostly replaced Frame Relay.
Full name: Asynchronous Transfer Mode.

children.title: MPLS
children.description:
Forwards packets based on short labels instead of looking up long network addresses.
Can encapsulate various protocols, including Frame Relay and ATM.
The dominant WAN protocol today.

nodes.title: Wireless
nodes.description:
We are moving steadily toward a wireless future: few people still use a landline phone, and laptops have lost most of their ports.
One of the biggest challenges with wireless is that signals are much easier to intercept. Instead of breaking into a building to connect to the corporate network, an attacker can sit in a van in the parking lot.
So encrypting wireless traffic is extremely important.

children.title: Wi-Fi
children.description:
The technology used everywhere to create local area networks without wires. (The Wi-Fi access point still plugs into a physical network.)
Range of about 100 meters.

children.title: Protocols
children.description:
IEEE (Institute of Electrical and Electronics Engineers) 802.11 is the family of standards used for wireless local area networks.
Many generations of 802.11 have been ratified over the last 20+ years.

children.title: 802.11a, b, g, n, ac, ax
children.description:
The generations of the 802.11 wireless LAN standard to recognize, from oldest to newest. The newest is branded Wi-Fi 6.
The versions show the evolution of the standard toward ever greater bandwidth and capabilities.

children.title: Encryption
children.description: Encrypting wireless traffic is critically important, because it is so much easier to eavesdrop on a wireless network.

children.title: WEP
children.description:
One of the first wireless encryption protocols, meant to give wireless networks the same privacy as cables. It does not live up to that.
It has very significant flaws in how it implements the RC4 encryption algorithm: the initialization vectors are far too short, so its encryption can be easily broken.
Never use it.
When the flaws were discovered, a quick band-aid was needed to prop it up until new wireless encryption protocols could be created and ratified.
Full name: Wired Equivalent Privacy.

children.title: TKIP
children.description:
The band-aid created for WEP: it still uses RC4, but mixes in a new key for every packet.
It has since been found to have significant flaws too, so do not use it.
Full name: Temporal Key Integrity Protocol.

children.title: WPA / WPA2
children.description:
- WPA: also an interim protocol, to deal with the WEP fiasco until the much better WPA2 could be ratified. WPA used TKIP for encryption by default.
- WPA2: uses the AES encryption algorithm by default. AES is much better than TKIP.

children.title: WiMAX
children.description:
A protocol for wireless Metropolitan Area Networks, with ranges of up to 90 kilometers.
Compare Wi-Fi, which creates local area networks with a range of about 100 meters.
The IEEE standard behind WiMAX.

children.title: GSM / CDMA
children.description:
Wireless radio protocols used by cellular companies to provide 2G and 3G voice and data services for mobile phones.
GSM has significant security issues:
- It is vulnerable to man-in-the-middle attacks. An attacker can create a rogue cell tower that phones connect to, and intercept communications.
- SIM (Subscriber Identity Module) cards can be cloned by extracting the user's IMSI (International Mobile Subscriber Identity). The attacker can then make and receive calls and receive the user's SMS messages. This cloning attack can be done over the air.
GSM and CDMA have largely been replaced by 4G / LTE, and now by 5G networks.
Full names: Global System for Mobile Communications; Code Division Multiple Access.

children.title: Microwave
children.description: A cost-effective way to create data links between buildings that are a few miles apart.

nodes.title: Internet Protocol (IP) Addresses
nodes.description:
The major way to make sure data sent across a network reaches the intended destination.
Think of an IP address as a postal address for a house: to send someone a letter, you need their address, and it must be unique to them. IP addresses serve the same function on a network.

children.title: IPv4 vs. IPv6
children.description:
IPv4 is the version used everywhere today. It has worked well for decades, but has big limitations:
- The address space is only 2^32: 4,294,967,296 possible addresses. When IPv4 was created, before the internet existed, 4.3 billion sounded like more than enough. With about 7.8 billion people (in 2020), many using several IP addresses each, it is not nearly enough.
- No security is built in by default.
IPv6 fixes both problems:
- The address space is 2^128: about 340 undecillion possible addresses.
- Encryption and integrity checking are built in. With IPv4, these capabilities had to be added on later.

children.title: IPv4 Network Classes
children.description:
IPv4 addresses are divided into five classes. You do not need to calculate subnet masks, but recognize the classes and the number of addresses in each:
- Class A: 2^24 = 16,777,216 addresses (16,777,214 usable).
- Class B: 2^16 = 65,536 addresses (65,534 usable).
- Class C: 2^8 = 256 addresses (254 usable).
- Class D: multicast addresses.
- Class E: reserved.

children.title: Private IPv4 Addresses
children.description:
Three ranges of IPv4 addresses are reserved for private networks, such as home and corporate networks:
- 10.0.0.0 to 10.255.255.255
- 172.16.0.0 to 172.31.255.255
- 192.168.0.0 to 192.168.255.255
Private addresses are NOT routable on the internet.

nodes.title: Converged Protocols
nodes.description:
Many specialty networks have been built over the years, such as the plain old telephone system, surveillance camera networks and storage area networks. Many needed proprietary protocols and dedicated networks.
Converged protocols run this specialty or proprietary traffic across a standard TCP/IP network instead. This removes the need for separate networks, which can be expensive to maintain.
Example: plug the security cameras or phones into the existing IP data network.

children.title: VoIP
children.description:
A perfect example of a converged protocol.
Telephone voice calls are sent as data across TCP/IP local area networks and the internet.

children.title: iSCSI, FCoE
children.description:
Two converged protocols for storing and retrieving data across a standard network:
- iSCSI: carries SCSI storage commands over IP networks, so remote storage looks like a local disk.
- FCoE: carries Fibre Channel storage area network traffic directly over Ethernet.

nodes.title: Network Authentication
nodes.description: Networks need authentication all the time, for example to authenticate a client to a server. Know these authentication protocols for the exam.

children.title: PAP
children.description:
One of the oldest authentication protocols.
Useless from a security perspective: the username and password are both sent in plaintext.
Full name: Password Authentication Protocol.

children.title: CHAP
children.description:
Sends authentication data in plaintext, but in a much cleverer way than PAP:
1. The server generates a random string, the challenge, and sends it to the client.
2. The client feeds its password and the challenge into the MD5 hashing algorithm, and sends the hash result to the server.
3. The server confirms that the user knows the password, without the password ever crossing the network in plaintext.
The hash can be sent in plaintext: hashing is a one-way function, so a man-in-the-middle cannot work out the password from it.
Full name: Challenge Handshake Authentication Protocol.

children.title: EAP
children.description:
Originally developed for PPP (Point-to-Point Protocol), but now widely used for authentication on wired LANs, wireless LANs and even WiMAX.
It is so widely used because it is extremely flexible: a framework on which many different authentication methods can run.
Common methods:
- EAP-TLS: client and server both authenticate with certificates. Security high, industry support high, not proprietary. Much more secure than EAP-MD5.
- EAP-TTLS: client uses ID & password, server uses a certificate. Security medium, industry support medium, proprietary (Certicom).
- EAP-PEAP: client uses ID & password, server uses a certificate. Security medium, industry support high, partly proprietary (Cisco, RSA & Microsoft).
- LEAP: client and server both use ID & password. Security low, industry support high, proprietary (Cisco).
- EAP-MD5: uses the MD5 hashing algorithm and is quite limited. Client uses ID & password, and there is no server authentication. Security low, industry support low, not proprietary.
Full name: Extensible Authentication Protocol.

children.title: PEAP
children.description:
Not a standalone authentication protocol: just a wrapper for EAP.
It encapsulates EAP inside an encrypted TLS (Transport Layer Security) tunnel, so any EAP traffic sent across the network is encrypted.

nodes.title: Network Attacks
nodes.description: Common types of network attacks, and how network attacks are generally carried out.

children.title: Phases
children.description: The four major phases of a network attack.

children.title: Reconnaissance
children.description:
Passive: only publicly available information is gathered, from sources such as job postings, LinkedIn profiles and DNS records.
The organization being attacked has no way to detect the attack in this phase.

children.title: Enumeration
children.description:
Active: the attacker systematically scans IP address ranges and ports, looking for live systems that offer services, as potential targets.
Because it is active, this is where an attack can start to be detected.

children.title: Vulnerability Analysis
children.description: The attacker tries to determine the exact version of a system and identify vulnerabilities that could be exploited.

children.title: Exploitation
children.description: The final phase: the attacker tries to exploit the vulnerabilities found.

children.title: Eavesdropping
children.description:
Passively listening to network traffic.
The prevailing network topology is bus, so an attacker connected to a wired or wireless network can usually listen in on traffic quite easily.

children.title: SYN Flooding
children.description: A form of denial-of-service attack. The attacker sends a rapid succession of TCP connection requests (the first step of the three-way handshake) to a target system and never completes the handshakes, trying to consume enough resources that it cannot respond to legitimate traffic.

children.title: IP Spoofing
children.description: The attacker changes the source IP address of a packet, either to hide their identity or to match another IP address on the network and pretend to be another system.

children.title: DoS / DDoS
children.description:
Any attack that harms the availability of the victim system, so that authorized users cannot use it for business purposes.
The distributed form: the same kind of attack from multiple attacking systems, possibly thousands, hundreds of thousands or even millions, all focused on making one target unavailable.

children.title: Man-in-the-Middle
children.description: The attacker places themselves between computers that are communicating with each other, so they can intercept or even modify the communications.

children.title: ARP poisoning
children.description:
The attacker sends forged replies that map their own MAC address to another system's IP address, such as the router's. Other systems store the false IP-to-MAC mapping in their tables and start sending that traffic to the attacker.
Example: traffic meant for the victim is sent to the attacker instead. A way to set up a man-in-the-middle attack.
Full name: Address Resolution Protocol.

nodes.title: Virtualization
nodes.description: Virtualization can segment networks logically and, with SDN, deliver strong security benefits.

children.title: VLAN
children.description:
Segments a network logically, through software, instead of physically by buying and configuring new network hardware.
One can be a subset of the ports on one switch, or subsets of ports on several switches, so systems can be separated into groups.
Network segmentation has many security benefits, and these are an efficient and economical way to achieve it.
Full name: Virtual Local Area Network.

children.title: SDN
children.description:
A massive leap in virtualization beyond simple VLANs. It creates multiple fully virtualized, software-controlled networks on top of a physical network.
Centralizing all control of the virtualized network gives far greater flexibility to reconfigure the network rapidly.
A critical part of what makes the cloud work.
It provides abstraction for network topology, network flow and network protocols.
Full name: Software Defined Network.

children.title: Northbound & Southbound APIs
children.description:
An SDN is split into three planes, linked by APIs:
- Application plane: network services such as load balancers and firewalls.
- Northbound APIs: connect the application plane to the control plane.
- Control plane: the SDN controller, the central brain of the network.
- Southbound APIs: connect the control plane to the data plane.
- Data plane: the switches and routers.

nodes.title: Common Commands
nodes.description: Some of the most common tools used to manage and maintain networks.

children.title: ipconfig
children.description: Shows the current TCP/IP network configuration of an endpoint, such as a computer: the IP and MAC addresses of every network interface card, plus the gateway, DHCP and DNS IP addresses.

children.title: ping
children.description: Tests whether a host on an IP network is reachable. Commonly used to see whether a system is online and responding.

children.title: traceroute
children.description: A network diagnostic tool that shows the route and transit delays of packets across an IP network: each hop on the way to the destination, with its response times.

children.title: whois
children.description: Queries databases that store the registered users of an internet resource, such as a domain name. Use it to find out who owns a domain name.

children.title: dig
children.description: Queries DNS (Domain Name System) for all the details of a domain name, such as the name servers and mail server it uses.
